newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. confident can win WTO Japan photo case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. confident can win WTO Japan photo case.

text.p: U.S. government officials and legal counsellors expressed confidence on Tuesday they would win a landmark case in the World Trade Organisation over what they argue is Japan's rigged photofilm market.

At briefings a day before the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) is expected to set up a panel to look into the complaint, they said they had amassed a wealth of evidence showing laws were shaped to favour Japan's Fuji company.

And they insisted that, although the row has been labelled "the Fuji-Kodak" case, the United States would be attacking Tokyo government regulations rather than the dominance the Japanese company holds on its domestic market.

"We believe we have a very strong case and that we can prove to a panel that a whole series of measures by the Japanese government going back many years is aimed at limiting market access in this sector for foreign products," an official of the U.S. Trade Representative's Office (USTR) in Geneva said.

And Rufus Yerxa, former deputy USTR and now a lawyer acting for Eastman Kodak, told a separate briefing the case would focus "on a whole group of laws that have been applied in to give less favourable treatment to imported goods."

The case is among five that will come before the DSB on Wednesday and one of three involving the four top trading powers -- the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada -- widely seen as likely to test the power of the fledgling WTO.

In another the EU, backed by Canada, will challenge the U.S. Helms-Burton law aimed at dissuading foreign firms from investing in Cuba by allowing them to be sued in U.S. courts and barring their executives access to the United States.

In the third, Canada will ask for -- and under the DSB's streamlined procedure -- will get a panel to look at whether the EU's 10-year ban on the import of hormone-treated beef is consistent with WTO free trade rules.

A panel has already been set up to look into a similar U.S. complaint, although the EU has struck back by challenging U.S. retaliation in the form of tariffs on European products as itself a violation of WTO agreements.

In two other cases, in both of which panels will be set up, Canada is challenging Brazilian subsidies for export of light aircraft and the U.S. is attacking Pakistan over what it sees as violations of WTO accords on patent protection.

The most explosive of these is the EU move to bring the Cuba issue -- a highly emotive topic in the United States -- before the WTO, a body many U.S. politicians argue should have no right to rule on sovereign decisions by Washington.

But no panel will be set up on Wednesday, unless the United States gives the go-ahead. Under DSB rules, it can block such a move at this stage since it will be the first time the EU will have brought the request to the body.

The WTO panel process, unlike that of its predecessor the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), sets a specific timeframe for disputes to be resolved and bars any country from blocking a final ruling by the collective WTO membership.

Initial panels have to hand down their rulings within six months but these can be appealed. The whole process from a decision to create the panel until a country found violating the rules is told to come into line can take up to 18 months.
